sections: Structure

The bone forming the prominence of the cheek. Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch; its frontal process forms the lateral margin of the orbit. Branches of the zygomatic nerve enter through the zygomatico-orbital foramen on its orbital surface and emerge to the skin of the cheek and temple.
clinical: In fractures of the zygomatic arch, temporalis and the coronoid process beneath can be trapped, restricting mouth opening.

facts: The opposite nasal bone, frontal bone, maxilla (frontal process), ethmoid (perpendicular plate)
tus: In nasal bone fractures a septal haematoma must be looked for; if not drained the septal cartilage undergoes necrosis.

clinical: Dacryocystorhinostomy (an operation opening the lacrimal sac into the nose) is performed through the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla.
In cleft palate the palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones fail to unite in the midline; it disturbs feeding and speech.

facts: Sphenoid, ethmoid (perpendicular plate), maxillae, palatine bones; its anterior border joins the septal cartilage
clinical: A deviated septum is mostly due to a bend at the junction of the vomer and the septal cartilage.
Hypertrophy of the inferior concha is a common cause of nasal obstruction; if medication fails the concha is reduced surgically.

sections: Structure

The atlas has no body and no spinous process; it is a ring made of an anterior and a posterior arch and two lateral masses. The dens of the axis fits into the facet on the back of the anterior arch and is held from behind by the transverse ligament of the atlas. The vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve (C1) run in the groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch.

facts: Transverse ligament of atlas (holds the dens from behind), alar ligaments (from the dens to the occipital condyles), apical ligament of dens, tectorial membrane
sections: Dens of axis
Embryologically it corresponds to the body of the atlas, fused to the axis. About half of the side-to-side turning of the head at the atlanto-axial joint takes place around this process.
Structure

A triangular bone formed by the fusion of five sacral vertebrae. Its anterior (pelvic) surface is concave; the anterior rami of the sacral spinal nerves leave through four pairs of anterior sacral foramina. On its posterior surface lie the median sacral crest (remnant of the spines) and, at its lower end, the sacral hiatus and sacral cornua. The front projection of its upper border is the promontory.
clinical: Caudal epidural anaesthesia is given through the sacral hiatus; the sacral cornua are the palpable landmarks for the needle.

facts: Gluteus maximus (posterior surface), coccygeus and the iliococcygeus part of levator ani (via the anococcygeal ligament)

sections: Structure and function

These extensions of hyaline cartilage join the ribs to the sternum and make the thoracic cage elastic. The 1st costal cartilage joins the sternum by a synarthrosis (synchondrosis), the 2nd–7th by synovial joints; the 8th–10th attach to the cartilage above and form the costal margin.
clinical: In Tietze syndrome there is painful swelling of the upper costal cartilages; costochondritis is chest wall pain without swelling and can be confused with cardiac pain.

sections: Structure

A horizontal, S-shaped long bone: its medial 2/3 is convex forwards and its lateral 1/3 concave forwards. The medial end articulates with the sternum, the lateral end with the acromion. On the inferior surface are the conoid tubercle and trapezoid line for the coracoclavicular ligament, the area for the costoclavicular ligament and the groove for subclavius. It has no medullary cavity.
Ends

Proximally the disc-shaped head of the radius articulates with the capitulum of the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna and is encircled by the annular ligament; below it lie the neck and the radial tuberosity, where biceps brachii attaches. The distal end is broad, with the radial styloid process laterally, the ulnar notch medially for the ulna and Lister's tubercle (dorsal tubercle) behind.
Ends

At the proximal end are the olecranon and the coronoid process, with the trochlear notch for the humerus between them and the radial notch laterally for the head of the radius. At the distal end the small head of the ulna and the ulnar styloid process are separated from the wrist joint by the triangular fibrocartilage disc.

facts: Vessels entering on its palmar and dorsal surfaces; in some people from a single source
sections: Position
A crescent-shaped bone lying in the lunate fossa of the radius in the middle of the proximal carpal row. It is the most frequently dislocated carpal bone.

facts: Lunate, pisiform, hamate; adjacent to the ulna through the triangular fibrocartilage disc
clinical: A dorsal avulsion fracture of the triquetrum is the second most common carpal fracture after the scaphoid; it occurs in falls on the back of the hand.
It is the least frequently fractured carpal bone, protected by its firm union with the base of the 2nd metacarpal.
Fractures of the capitate are rare, but because the vessels to its head are retrograde, avascular necrosis can develop.
In lunate dislocation the capitate stays in line with the radius while the lunate tips forwards (distinguished from perilunate dislocation).

sections: Hook of hamate

A hook-shaped projection towards the palm; it is the medial attachment of the flexor retinaculum and the lateral wall of Guyon's canal. Flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi attach to it.

clinical: A pisiform fracture usually results from a direct fall on the hypothenar region and can affect the nearby ulnar nerve.

sections: Structure

Each metacarpal has a base proximally, a body (shaft) in the middle and a head distally. The heads form the 'knuckles' when the fist is clenched. The first metacarpal is the shortest and thickest; its saddle joint with the trapezium allows opposition of the thumb.
tus: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the 1st metacarpal; abductor pollicis longus pulls the distal fragment proximally.

sections: Structure

Each phalanx has a base, a shaft and a head. The bases of the proximal phalanges articulate with the metacarpal heads, the others with the head of the phalanx before. At the tip of each distal phalanx is the ungual tuberosity, which supports the nail bed.
Structure

A triangular sesamoid bone with its base above and apex below. Its front surface is covered by fibres of the quadriceps tendon; its back surface has thick cartilage and is divided by a vertical ridge into medial and lateral facets that sit in the groove between the femoral condyles (patellar surface). The lateral facet is the larger.
Ends

The proximal end is broad: medial and lateral condyles, with the intercondylar area and eminence between them, where the cruciate ligaments and menisci attach. In front is the tibial tuberosity for the patellar ligament. At the distal end are the medial malleolus and the fibular notch.
Function

It contributes little to weight-bearing (about 10–15%); its main roles are to give attachment to muscles and, distally, to form the lateral wall of the ankle joint with the lateral malleolus. The middle part of its shaft can be taken as a graft.

facts: Mainly the artery of the tarsal canal (from the posterior tibial) and the artery of the tarsal sinus (from the dorsalis pedis); blood flows retrogradely from the neck to the body
sections: Parts

It consists of the head (articulating with the navicular), neck and body. The trochlea on the upper surface of the body is wider in front than behind, so the ankle is more stable in dorsiflexion. The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs in the groove between the medial and lateral tubercles of the posterior process.

facts: Calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, plantaris, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor hallucis, abductor digiti minimi, quadratus plantae, extensor digitorum brevis
sections: Main features

Behind is the calcaneal tuberosity (heel), medially the sustentaculum tali carrying the talus (the FHL tendon passes beneath it), laterally the fibular trochlea separating the tendons of the fibular muscles. The upper surface has three facets for the talus with the calcaneal groove between them; together with the groove of the talus it forms the sinus tarsi.

facts: Talus (head of talus), three cuneiforms, sometimes the cuboid
sections: Clinical relevance

It lies near the top of the medial arch. Its tuberosity is felt in front of and below the medial malleolus. Some people have an accessory navicular, which can cause pain through traction of the tibialis posterior tendon.

facts: Calcaneus, lateral cuneiform, navicular (sometimes), 4th and 5th metatarsals
On the inferior surface the groove for the fibularis longus tendon and the cuboid tuberosity in front of it
clinical: Cuboid syndrome, a slight displacement of the cuboid causing pain along the lateral border of the foot, is seen especially in dancers.
Cuneiform fractures are rare; they usually accompany a Lisfranc injury.
tus: The medial cuneiform is the largest and the intermediate the smallest; the shortness of the intermediate cuneiform locks the base of the 2nd metatarsal.

sections: Structure

The phalanges of the foot are much shorter than those of the hand; the middle and distal phalanges of the 2nd–5th toes are especially small and in the 5th toe often fused. The phalanges of the big toe (hallux) are thick and strong; they are the last point through which weight passes in the push-off phase of walking.
